etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Doublet of cursus and cour.

definitions.definition: A normal or customary sequence.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: The course of true love never did run smooth.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book X”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Day and night, / Seedtime and harvest, heat and hoary frost, / Shall hold their course.

definitions.definition: A programme, a chosen manner of proceeding.
Any ordered process or sequence of steps.

quote.citation: 1958 September 6, Weasel While You Work, spoken by the Barnyard Dawg:
quote.text: There is but one course for me to follow: I'LL MOIDER THE BUM!

definitions.definition: a series of lectures or lessons in a particular subject
(UK, Ireland) an educational programme at a college or university leading to an academic degree or vocational qualification.

quote.citation: 1661, John Fell, The Life of the most learned, reverend and pious Dr. H. Hammond‎[2]:
quote.text: During the whole time of his abode in the university he generally spent thirteen hours of the day in study; by which assiduity besides an exact dispatch of the whole course of philosophy, he read over in a manner all classic authors that are extant […]

definitions.definition: (education) A learning programme

quote.text: Her course will be ‘Communication Studies with Theatre Studies’: God, how tedious, how pointless.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “The attack of the MOOCs”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Since the launch early last year of […] two Silicon Valley start-ups offering free education through MOOCs, massive open online courses, the ivory towers of academia have been shaken to their foundations. University brands built in some cases over centuries have been forced to contemplate the possibility that information technology will rapidly make their existing business model obsolete.

definitions.definition: (especially in medicine) A treatment plan.

quote.text: Miss Clark, alarmed at her increasing stoutness, was doing a course of what is popularly known as banting.

definitions.definition: (cooking) A stage of a meal.
The succession of one to another in office or duty; order; turn.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Chronicles 8:14:
quote.text: He appointed  […]  the courses of the priests.

definitions.definition: A sequence of events.
The itinerary of a race.
A racecourse.
The path taken by a flow of water; a watercourse.
(sports) The trajectory of a ball, frisbee etc.
(golf) A golf course.
(nautical) The direction of movement of a vessel at any given moment.
(navigation) The intended passage of voyage, such as a boat, ship, airplane, spaceship, etc.
(India, historical) The drive usually frequented by Europeans at an Indian station.

quote.citation: 1853, William Delafield Arnold, Oakfield; or, Fellowship in the East, section II, page 124:
quote.text: It was curious to Oakfield to be back on the Ferozepore course, after a six months' interval, which seemed like years. How much had happened in these six months!

definitions.definition: A path that something or someone moves along.
(nautical) The lowest square sail in a fully rigged mast, often named according to the mast.
(in the plural, courses, obsolete, euphemistic) Menses.

quote.citation: 2018, Gail Kern Paster, The  Body Embarrassed‎[3], Cornell University, page 92:
quote.text: The bleeding body signifies as a shameful token of uncontrol, as a failure of physical self-mastery particularly associated with woman in her monthly "courses".

definitions.definition: (masonry) A row of bricks or blocks.
(roofing) A row of material that forms the roofing, waterproofing or flashing system.
(textiles) In weft knitting, a single row of loops connecting the loops of the preceding and following rows.
A row or file of objects.
(music) One or more strings on some musical instruments (such as the guitar, lute or vihuela): if multiple, then closely spaced, tuned in unison or octaves and intended to be played together.
To run or flow (especially of liquids and more particularly blood).

quote.citation: 2001, Salman Rushdie, Fury: A Novel, London: Jonathan Cape, →ISBN, page 5:
quote.text: Sudden anger rose in him. “What I’m looking for,” he barked, “is to be left in peace.” His voice trembled with a rage far bigger than her intrusion merited, the rage which shocked him whenever it coursed through his nervous system, like a flood.

quote.citation: 2013 September 20, Martina Hyde, “Is the pope Catholic?”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: He is a South American, so perhaps revolutionary spirit courses through Francis's veins. But what, pray, does the Catholic church want with doubt?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To run through or over.
(transitive) To pursue by tracking or estimating the course taken by one's prey; to follow or chase after.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene vi]:
quote.text: We coursed him at the heels.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to chase after or pursue game.
(colloquial) Ellipsis of of course.

quote.citation: 1922, A. M. Chisholm, A Thousand a Plate:
quote.text: "Course it's mighty hard to tell till we've put out a few traps," said the former, "but it looks to me like we've struck it lucky."

quote.citation: 1946, Milton “Mezz” Mezzrow, Bernard Wolfe, “Tell a Green Man Something”, in Really the Blues, New York, N.Y.: Random House, book 3 (1928–1935: The Big Apple), page 209:
quote.text: Course, my home wasn't exactly in Harlem  […]
